verifiedClaims.claim: The 1892 Columbian half dollar was the first commemorative coin produced by the U.S. Mint and marked the exposition’s planned four-hundredth anniversary celebration.
Public Law 203 authorized up to five million silver half dollars and connected payment to documented exposition preparation expenses and financial conditions.
The obverse depicts Columbus in profile; the reverse shows the Santa Maria and two globes; Charles Barber and George Morgan are credited for the respective designs.
The fair opened in 1893 while the commemorative coin law was enacted in 1892; the Mint later issued a Queen Isabella quarter in 1893.

stats.statement: The 1892 act authorized up to five million coins using uncurrent subsidiary silver, with proceeds tied to exposition labor and material costs and financial conditions set by Congress.

stats.statement: The Mint calls the Columbian half dollar its first commemorative coin and identifies the 1893 Queen Isabella quarter as the next commemorative issue.
Charles Barber designed the Columbus obverse and George Morgan the reverse showing the Santa Maria between two globes.
The act supported exposition preparation expenses before opening, with payment conditioned on documented fair funding and eligible costs.
